summary:
Shanyraq: Call Home is a browser and mobile game for kids aged 7 to 12. The player wakes up alone on a Mars base in Gale Crater after a solar storm has cut it off from the crew and from Earth. To get everyone back together, they restore power, repair the antenna and relay, protect the crew from a solar particle storm and finally call Earth.

The challenge asks kids to think like astronauts. Our game does this by making every decision a real trade-off: heating, oxygen and air scrubbing all draw on the same limited power, and water used for radiation shielding is water you can’t drink or turn into oxygen. The temperatures, radiation, oxygen production, dust storms and signal delay are all based on NASA mission data. Solar flares come live from NASA DONKI.

It matters because most kids only ever watch space. Here they actually manage it, in English, Russian or Kazakh, on any device, even offline.
details:
What it does. A side-view pixel-art adventure in four acts.

  • The player explores the base, a landed ship and a crater ridge.
  • They talk to the crew and to HermX, a helper robot.
  • They solve short repair puzzles: power budget, cable routing, antenna alignment, rover route energy, radiation shielding.
  • Repairs also bring back pieces of the hero’s lost memory.

How it works.

  • The base runs in real time; one game hour is 6 to 9 seconds.
    • solar output depends on time of day, dust on the panels and dust in the air (optical depth);
    • indoor temperature follows heat loss to the outside;
    • O₂ and CO₂ change with the number of people and the equipment that is on;
    • radiation dose depends on where you are and how much soil and water shield you.
  • Going over the 9 kW breaker limit causes a blackout.
  • To keep it manageable for kids, the screen shows only three systems: power, life support and shielding.

Benefits.

  • Kids learn real constraints by playing, not reading.
  • Every science fact in the dialogue opens a small “Real Science” panel with the source and a link.
  • Two difficulty levels: Cadet (7 to 9) and Engineer (10 to 12).
  • Three languages: English, Russian, Kazakh.
  • Works offline after loading.

Intended impact. Free and easy to use in classrooms, including schools with weak internet. We plan to test it with children in Kazakhstan and add a group mode where each kid plays a crew role.

Tools.

  • The game: HTML5 Canvas, JavaScript and CSS, built into one self-contained file with a Python build script.
  • The app: Flutter (Dart) with webview_flutter and url_launcher, for Android and iOS.
  • Testing: Playwright for automated full playthroughs, Pillow for image processing.
  • Fonts: Handjet and Tiny5 (Google Fonts, Open Font License).
  • Art: the hand-drawn hero and the other artwork were drawn by hand; the pixel art is drawn in code.

Creativity.

  • Science is built into a story with characters kids care about.
  • Repairs unlock memories, and every choice has a cost.
  • Kazakh culture is part of the design: the base is named after the shanyraq, the crown of a yurt, and the ship carries Kazakh ornaments.
  • The game has 23 achievements and hidden easter eggs, for example jumping in Mars gravity, a chess puzzle and finding Earth in the night sky.
  • The sprites of the main character and some drawings inside the game are hand-drawn.

Factors we considered.

  • Age-appropriate difficulty.
  • Not overloading kids with too many systems.
  • Scientific accuracy in simple words.
  • Making sure no choice is free.
  • Readability and touch controls.
  • Offline play, multiple languages, and avoiding stereotypes in the characters.
